subject: Chemistry
title: Immunotherapy: Unleashing the Immune System
description: Learn Immunotherapy: Unleashing the Immune System in one minute.

hook.text: Cancer cells hide from your immune system by pressing a 'don't eat me' button on immune cells. Immunotherapy blocks that button.

buildup.text: T cells patrol the body for threats. But they have checkpoint receptors (PD-1, CTLA-4) that cancer exploits to avoid attack.

discovery.text: Checkpoint inhibitors block these 'off switches.' With the brakes released, T cells recognize and destroy cancer cells.

twist.text: James Allison and Tasuku Honjo won the 2018 Nobel Prize for this discovery. Their work was rejected by journals for years.

climax.text: Immunotherapy has cured some metastatic melanomas—previously 100% fatal. Not all patients respond, but those who do can be cured.

punchline.text: Release the brakes on immunity. Your body already knows how to kill cancer.

quiz.question: How do cancer cells evade the immune system?
options: They activate checkpoint receptors on T cells that act as 'off switches' for immune attack
They release chemicals that destroy all nearby immune cells
They mutate so rapidly that the immune system can't recognize them

details.summary: Cancer immunotherapy uses drugs called checkpoint inhibitors that block proteins like PD-1 and CTLA-4 that cancer cells exploit to hide from the immune system. Removing these molecular brakes allows T cells to recognize and destroy tumors that previously evaded immune surveillance.
details.whyItMatters: Immunotherapy earned the 2018 Nobel Prize and has produced durable complete remissions in previously terminal cancers. It represents a fundamental shift from attacking cancer directly to empowering the immune system.
takeaways: Cancer cells use checkpoint proteins to suppress immune T cell attacks
Checkpoint inhibitors remove these brakes, unleashing T cells against tumors
Some patients achieve complete long-term remission from terminal cancers

faq.question: Why doesn't the immune system destroy cancer cells on its own?
faq.answer: Cancer cells evolve mechanisms to evade immune detection. They express checkpoint proteins like PD-L1 that bind immune cell PD-1 receptors, sending a do-not-attack signal. Some cancer cells also downregulate surface markers that T cells use for recognition, becoming essentially invisible.

faq.question: Why does immunotherapy only work for some cancer patients?
faq.answer: Response depends on the tumor's mutation burden, which generates recognizable antigens, its checkpoint protein expression, and the patient's pre-existing immune response. Tumors with more mutations tend to be more immunogenic. Research is ongoing to predict responders and convert non-responders.
